item.title: Jackson Police Searching for 2 Missing Females Reported as Runaways - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Morgan Howard
item.description:
JACKSON – The Jackson Police Department is asking for the public’s help in locating two females who have been reported as runaways.

Police said they are searching for 16-year-old Jazzlynn Kimble, who is described as 5 feet 6 inches tall and weighing about 150 pounds.

Authorities are also searching for 18-year-old Kaitlyn Santin, who is described as 5 feet 2 inches tall, weighing about 165 pounds, with brown hair and brown eyes.

According to police, both ran away from 805 Flag Chapel Road in Jackson.

Anyone with information about the whereabouts of either Jazzlynn Kimble or Kaitlyn Santin is asked to contact the Jackson Police Department at 601-906-7068.

item.title: Warrior Bonfire Program to host fishing tournament April 18 - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Therese Apel
item.description:
PEARL — Anglers and community members are invited to gather April 18 at the Ross Barnett Reservoir for a day of fishing and fundraising aimed at supporting Purple Heart recipients.

The Warrior Bonfire Crappie Tournament is scheduled to begin with lines in at 6:30 a.m., with participants launching from most public ramps around the reservoir. Registration closes at 7:30 a.m., and fishing will continue until 2 p.m., followed by a 3:30 p.m. weigh-in at Bass Pro Shops.

Organizers say proceeds from the tournament will benefit the Warrior Bonfire Program, a nonprofit that provides outdoor retreats and long-term support for post-9/11 Purple Heart recipients.

The event will feature a five-fish limit per boat, with prizes awarded to the top three finishers. First place will receive a $300 gift card and trophy, followed by $200 and $100 gift cards for second and third place, respectively. An optional “Big Fish Pot” will also be available, with a payout for the largest catch.

Beyond the competition, the event is designed as a community gathering to honor veterans and raise awareness of the program’s mission. The Warrior Bonfire Program focuses on activity-based, stress-free experiences that promote camaraderie and healing for service members wounded in combat.

Those who do not fish can still participate through a raffle open nationwide. Tickets are $20 each or six for $100, with prizes including Bass Pro Shops gift cards ranging from $100 to $500 and nearly two dozen additional giveaways. Winners will be announced during the weigh-in, and participants do not need to be present to win.

See the Warrior Bonfire Program on Amazon Prime

Event organizers said attendees can expect live updates throughout the day, an emcee, and appearances from local sponsors and the Mississippi Army National Guard. Food will also be available at the weigh-in, with Penn’s Fish House food truck serving fish and chicken.

Fishing is not permitted to launch from Madison Landing or Goshen Springs, but all other public ramps at the reservoir are open for the tournament.

Organizers said the event aims to combine outdoor recreation with a meaningful cause, emphasizing that “no warrior heals alone.”

item.title: Spring Cleaning Your Kitchen? Here's How to Keep Bugs Out - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Special to Darkhorse Press
item.description:
(StatePoint) With warmer weather here, spring cleaning and hosting season are in full swing. While you prep your home for guests, you may also be seeing an uptick of insect activity.

Unfortunately, insects tend to gather in the same areas of the home where household members and guests do – anywhere there is food. So, rather than let bugs disrupt your spring gatherings, act right away. Doing so is important, as insects reproduce rapidly. In fact, it only takes one week for two fruit flies to multiply to 500 fruit flies!

By using these tips to banish bugs from your kitchen this spring, you can enjoy the feeling you get when your space is truly clean and guest-ready:

Do a deep clean: In addition to regular kitchen upkeep, be sure to do a deep clean in spring and every time you host. This is a great way to finally tackle those corners, crevices and seldom-addressed surfaces in the fridge, oven and pantry, where pest-attracting food residue and grease can build up.

Catch what you can’t clean: A fly trap for indoors is a necessary addition to your kitchen spring cleaning and hosting routine. Zevo catches what you can’t clean – working continuously to trap those pesky flies and gnats that linger around sinks, trash cans, and countertops even after you’ve scrubbed. Simply plug in a Zevo Flying Insect Trap near high-traffic areas, such as near party spreads, fruit bowls or garbage, and doors that are opened throughout the day. Its blue and UV light attract and catch fruit flies, gnats, house flies and other flying insects 24/7 and its sleek, discreet design will look good in your kitchen.

“Plugging in a Zevo Insect Trap is an easy way to achieve that level of cleanliness you’re looking for, so you have more time for what matters – enjoying the spring season with friends and family,” says Rob Reinerman, Vice President of Procter & Gamble Ventures, parent company of Zevo, a line of worry-free pest solutions.

Fix leaks: If you have a leak under your kitchen sink, you may unwittingly be creating an inviting habitat for bugs, which are drawn to water sources. Fix the leak so you invite only human guests to your kitchen and home this spring. Doing so will have the added benefit of preventing water damage and mold.

Seal food tightly: Take a quick look at your pantry to assess your food storage containers. Transfer all items like flour and sugar out of paper packaging and into tightly-sealed jars. Not only will this help keep bugs at bay, but your essential ingredients will stay fresher for improved hosting.

For more information about pest control in the kitchen and other areas of your home, visit zevoinsect.com.

Maintaining a tidy kitchen is just the first step in banishing bugs. Simple additional measures that require very little effort can help you truly keep the spaces where you prep, host, and enjoy your food clean, fresh and insect-free.

item.title: New Beer’s Eve taps into history, celebration across Mississippi and beyond - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Therese Apel
item.description:
MISSISSIPPI — Before the first pour of National Beer Day on April 7, we raise a glass the night before, celebrating New Beer’s Eve, a holiday rooted in one of the most dramatic turnarounds in U.S. history.

Observed each year on April 6, New Beer’s Eve marks the moment in 1933 when legal beer returned after more than a decade of Prohibition. According to NationalToday.com, President Franklin D. Roosevelt ushered in the change, allowing Americans to once again drink, buy and sell alcohol legally.

The result was immediate and enthusiastic. NationalToday.com reports that Americans consumed about 1.5 million gallons of beer in the first 24 hours after Prohibition effectively ended, with crowds lining up outside bars and taverns for their first legal drink in nearly 13 years.

The celebration was about more than just beer, it was about connection and communication in a changing country. According to DaysOfTheYear.com, people gathered in pubs, restaurants and homes, eager to reconnect over a simple pleasure that had been banned since 1920 under the 18th Amendment.

Prohibition, which lasted from 1920 to 1933, outlawed the production and sale of alcohol nationwide. Britannica.com notes the ban created widespread demand for faster policy change as the nation faced economic hardship during the Great Depression and sought new sources of jobs and tax revenue.

When restrictions were lifted, even partially at first with low-alcohol beer, it jumpstarted breweries and related industries. Historical accounts cited by DaysOfTheYear.com indicate the return of beer helped revive manufacturing, agriculture and transportation sectors tied to brewing.

Today, New Beer’s Eve is celebrated in a much lighter spirit, often with tastings, brewery tours and gatherings with friends. DaysOfTheYear.com suggests hosting beer tastings, trying local brews or visiting a nearby brewery as popular ways to mark the occasion.

Across the country, breweries and beer brands often join in the celebration. National brands like Anheuser-Busch, which famously delivered beer to the White House in 1933 using its iconic Clydesdales, continue to lean into the holiday through promotions tied to National Beer Day.

Closer to home, Mississippi’s growing craft beer scene offers its own way to celebrate. Breweries such as Lazy Magnolia Brewing Company in Kiln and Southern Prohibition Brewing in Hattiesburg have helped fuel the state’s craft beer boom, reflecting a national shift toward more diverse and locally brewed options. NationalToday.com notes craft beer has surged in popularity in recent decades as drinkers seek new flavors and styles.

Beer itself has a long and global history, dating back thousands of years. NationalToday.com says evidence of early barley beer dates to around 3400 B.C., and ancient civilizations such as the Babylonians and Egyptians even incorporated beer into daily life and labor systems.

Despite its ancient roots, modern beer culture continues to evolve. From light lagers to bold craft brews, the variety available today would have been unimaginable during Prohibition.

Health experts still emphasize moderation. NationalToday.com defines moderate drinking as up to one drink per day for women and up to two for men.

For many, though, New Beer’s Eve is less about quantity and more about appreciating history, community and a cold drink shared among friends.

After all, as Roosevelt reportedly remarked when beer made its return in 1933, it was simply “a good time for a beer.”

item.title: MSDH Recognizes National Public Health Week Across Mississippi - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Morgan Howard
item.description:
The Mississippi State Department of Health is joining agencies and organizations across the country in recognizing National Public Health Week from April 6-12.

According to MSDH, the observance highlights the important role public health professionals play in protecting and improving the health of communities across the state.

The department said public health workers, including nurses, physicians, epidemiologists, inspectors and community health workers, make an impact in every part of Mississippi.

Throughout the week, MSDH said it will highlight a number of services that support Mississippi families each day. Those include perinatal and infant services, child and adolescent services, adult health, vital records and statistics, regulatory services, WIC, communicable disease prevention, county health departments, rural health and physician workforce programs, EMS and acute care systems, the opioid and substance use program, epidemiology and the Mississippi Medical Cannabis Program.

MSDH is encouraging the public to follow along through the MSDH Healthy Mobile App and on its website for updates during the week.

item.title: MISSING IN MISSISSIPPI: Emmanuel Williams, Choctaw County - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Therese Apel
item.description:
CHOCTAW COUNTY — A year and a few months after he was last heard from, very little is known about what happened to Emmanuel Williams, and those who love him are still searching for answers.

Williams, 38, has been missing since December 2024, according to information from Missingsippi.org, a nonprofit that tracks missing persons cases across the state. He was last in contact with family members in Ackerman around that time and has not been heard from since.

Described as a Black male with black hair and brown eyes, Williams is about 5 feet 8 inches tall and weighs approximately 140 pounds. His sudden disappearance and lack of communication understandably raised concerns among loved ones.

According to Missingsippi.org, Williams has ties to the Little Rock, Arkansas, area and could possibly be there. However, no confirmed sightings or updates about his whereabouts have been publicly reported.

With very few details available online or in a search of Newspapers.com, his case highlights the uncertainty many families face when a loved one goes missing. There is no publicly released information that can be easily found about the circumstances surrounding his disappearance.

Williams’ family remains concerned for his safety and is hoping someone may have seen him or has information that could help bring him home.

Anyone with information about Emmanuel Williams is encouraged to contact [email protected] .

As time passes, advocates say sharing the little-known cases like Williams’ is critical to keeping attention on missing persons across Mississippi and helping bring them home.

item.title: Laurel man arrested in connection with Howard Industries arson - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Cash Matlock
item.description:
LAUREL — A Laurel man wanted in connection with a vehicle fire at an industrial site has been arrested, authorities said.

The Jones County Sheriff’s Department initially sought Rashad Lawrence, 30, on a charge of arson following a March 31, 2026, incident at Howard Industries in the Pendorff community.

Deputies and the Laurel Fire Department responded to reports of a vehicle fire at the facility, where investigators later determined that three passenger vehicles in the parking lot had been damaged. Authorities identified Lawrence as the suspect.

The sheriff’s department had asked the public for help locating Lawrence and said a financial reward could be available through Jones County Crime Stoppers for information leading to his arrest.

In an update, officials said Lawrence has since been taken into custody. According to the sheriff’s department, he peacefully surrendered to Deputy Jarone Walker at a residence in the Currie community.

The arrest stems from the ongoing investigation into the March 31 vehicle fire at Howard Industries.

No additional details about charges or court proceedings were immediately released.

item.title: Jackson to receive $26.5M in state projects for roads, parks, arts and infrastructure - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Therese Apel
item.description:
JACKSON — More than $26 million in state-funded projects are headed to Jackson, targeting roads, parks, infrastructure and cultural institutions across the capital city and Hinds County.

City officials announced the funding, included in Senate Bill 2189, the 2026 legislative projects bill, will bring approximately $26.52 million in total appropriations within Jackson city limits.

Of that, about $5.67 million will go directly to City of Jackson projects, including road paving, park improvements and neighborhood infrastructure work. The largest portion, $19 million, will support local nonprofit organizations focused on recreation, education and the arts.

Hinds County is also set to receive more than $7.2 million in additional funding, with about $1.85 million of that benefiting projects within Jackson.

Mayor John Horhn praised the collaboration between city leaders, lawmakers and state officials.

“Jackson is moving forward because so many people rolled up their sleeves and went to work for our city,” Horhn said. “When we stay at the table and keep advocating for Jackson, we can deliver results for our residents.”

Among the city-funded projects, $4 million is designated as matching funds for federal highway and road improvements along key corridors including Woodrow Wilson Avenue, Medgar Evers Boulevard and McDowell Road. Other allocations include $750,000 for infrastructure improvements in northwest Jackson, $400,000 for Westside community projects and $200,000 to pave a portion of Hanging Moss Road.

Parks and recreation projects will also see investment, including $250,000 for upgrades to the Pete Brown Golf Facility and $70,000 for tree removal at Leavell Woods and Sykes Park.

A significant portion of the funding will support nonprofit partners. LeFleur’s Bluff Conservancy is set to receive $13 million for improvements at LeFleur’s Bluff State Park, while Mississippi Children’s Museum will receive $5 million to expand exhibits and programming. Additional funding includes $650,000 for the Mississippi Museum of Art and $350,000 for the Mississippi Symphony Orchestra to support music programs.

Regional projects funded through Hinds County include $500,000 for sewer and drainage improvements in the Presidential Hills neighborhood, $100,000 for neighborhood security cameras in several Jackson communities and $750,000 for repairs at Parham Bridges Park.

The Jackson Municipal Airport Authority will also receive $500,000 in matching funds for infrastructure upgrades.

Horhn also credited local partners, including the Jackson City Council, Hinds County Board of Supervisors and community organizations, for helping secure the funding.

While noting ongoing challenges such as long-term infrastructure needs, Horhn said the investment signals continued progress for the city.

item.title: Jackson State launches Industry Access Series with Lionsgate executive - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Therese Apel
item.description:
JACKSON — Jackson State University will launch a new speaker series Tuesday aimed at connecting students with industry leaders, beginning with a conversation featuring a top Hollywood marketing executive.

The inaugural session of “THEE Industry Access Series: From JXN to the Industry” will feature Briana McElroy, executive vice president and head of worldwide digital marketing at Lionsgate. The event is scheduled for 11 a.m. to noon in the Dollye M.E. Robinson Liberal Arts Building on campus.

University officials said the series is designed to give students and the Jackson community direct access to professionals across a range of fields, offering mentorship, career insight and networking opportunities that connect classroom learning to real-world experience.

Tuesday’s discussion will highlight McElroy’s career path from Jackson to a senior leadership role in the film industry, as well as her work on major movie marketing campaigns. Organizers said the conversation will also explore the impact of historically Black colleges and universities and community ties on career development.

The session will be moderated by Callie Callicut, a Jackson State senior majoring in journalism and media studies and a member of the university’s women’s track and field team.

Jackson State is hosting the event as part of its Research Engagement Week. Officials said students attending will gain insight into how large-scale film campaigns are developed and what it takes to break into the entertainment industry.

McElroy currently leads digital marketing strategy for major film releases, including projects that have incorporated HBCU culture, such as marching band performances.

The event is open to students, faculty and the community, and light refreshments will be provided, according to the university.

item.title: Former Southeast Greene Water Authority Manager Arrested on Embezzlement Charge - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Morgan Howard
item.description:
SOUTHEAST GREENE – A former office manager for the Southeast Greene Water Authority has been arrested on allegations that she embezzled money from the water authority for personal use, according to the Mississippi Office of the State Auditor.

State Auditor Shad White announced that special agents with his office arrested Deborah Harper, the former office manager, in connection with the case.

item.title: Adams County man arrested for allegedly hitting girlfriend in the face with a gun - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Morgan Howard
item.description:
NATCHEZ – A Natchez man is facing multiple charges after deputies say he assaulted his girlfriend with a firearm and drove away in her vehicle early Sunday morning.

Sheriff Travis Patten said the Adams County Sheriff’s Office takes domestic violence cases seriously and remains committed to protecting victims and holding offenders accountable.

The sheriff’s office also praised the victim for reporting the abuse, saying her decision to come forward may have prevented further violence.

item.title: Retired educator identified as victim in Adams County homicide investigation - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Morgan Howard
item.description:
ADAMS COUNTY – The Adams County Sheriff’s Office has released new details in an ongoing homicide investigation that began with a welfare check earlier Friday on Melanie Road.

Authorities identified the victim as Lana Brown Bradley, a retired educator and longtime member of the Adams County community.

In a statement, the sheriff’s office said Bradley was a respected figure whose death has deeply affected the community.

Investigators have confirmed the case is a homicide. Officials said details about the victim’s condition are being withheld out of respect for the family and to protect the integrity of the investigation.

A person who had previously been identified as a person of interest has now been named a suspect, according to the sheriff’s office. That person remains in custody at the Adams County Sheriff’s Office while investigators continue working the case.

The Adams County Sheriff’s Office is leading the investigation with assistance from the Mississippi Bureau of Investigation.

Sheriff Travis Patten described the case as one of the most difficult of his career.

“In my entire career, this is one of the most difficult and heartbreaking cases I have encountered,” Patten said in a statement. “Our hearts are with the family of Ms. Bradley, and we are committed to pursuing justice on their behalf.”

The investigation remains active, and officials said additional information will be released as it becomes available.

The sheriff’s office asked the public to keep Bradley’s family in their thoughts and prayers.

item.title: Darkhorse Press announces inaugural Blue Shield Award winners at Big Buck Bounty breakfast - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Darkhorse Press
item.description:
MISSISSIPPI — Darkhorse Press presented its inaugural Blue Shield Awards Saturday morning at a breakfast ceremony held in conjunction with Digio Strategies’ Big Buck Bounty, recognizing five Mississippi cases and the officers whose acts of courage, compassion, and dedication exemplify the best of public service.

The awards were given by Darkhorse Press, The Legend 93.5, and Rock 93.1, and sponsored by Southern Connection Police Supplies. Darkhorse Press Executive Editor Therese Apel presented each award to the honorees.

“Heroism is hard to encapsulate because it looks like so many different things,” Apel said. “But one thing it always looks like is selflessness. Each of these five honorees showed that in a different way, and every one of them deserves to be recognized.”

The following officers were named as the 2025 Blue Shield Award recipients:

Deputy Martin Luther Shields, Jr. — Hinds County Sheriff’s Department (Posthumous)

The Blue Shield Award was presented posthumously to Deputy Martin Luther Shields, Jr., 37, who was killed in the line of duty in February 2025.

Shields responded to a domestic call to escort a woman and her friend to a home to retrieve belongings. Officials said the responding officers were ambushed by the woman’s husband, Eric Brown, 42, who opened fire with a fully automatic weapon.

Shields was killed. The two women were also shot but survived. Brown subsequently took his own life.

Shields had previously served with the Jackson Police Department, where he received the department’s “I Am The City of Jackson” award for saving a life. Colleagues described him as dependable, courageous, and deeply committed to the communities he served.

He is survived by his wife, Kristian, and his daughter, Aubrey.

At a celebration of life held at the Jackson Revival Center, Gov. Tate Reeves said Shields “represents the best of Mississippi” and told his family, “We are all safer because of him and his courage.” Hinds County Sheriff Tyree Jones said Shields treated public service not as a job but as a calling, and told Aubrey Shields she is “destined for greatness.”

“We cannot give you back what was taken from you. But we can stand here and say, in front of everyone in this room, that what Martin did matters. That it will not be forgotten,” Apel said. “That Darkhorse Press, and every partner whose name is on this award, is committed to making sure Mississippi knows who Martin Luther Shields, Jr. was.”

The award was accepted by Shields’ mother, Marcy Levy, and other members of his family, on behalf of the Martin Luther Shields Jr. Memorial Foundation .

Sgt. Brian Brock — DeSoto County Sheriff’s Department

Brock, 35, was honored for an act of selfless heroism on Interstate 269 in which he deliberately drove his patrol vehicle into the path of a wrong-way driver to protect other motorists.

Reports came in that a vehicle was traveling westbound in the eastbound lanes at high speed. As other deputies pursued from behind, Brock was positioned ahead of the oncoming car. When he saw the headlights approaching from the wrong direction, he made a decision that DeSoto County Sheriff Thomas Tuggle said should have cost Brock his life.

“Then he said these words that should be remembered as long as people in this state talk about the meaning of courage: ‘This is it for me, but I’m going to do it,'” Apel said. “Then he drove his patrol vehicle head-on into the path of the oncoming car.”

The driver directly behind Brock, a physician, was shielded from the collision. Brock sustained serious injuries but survived. Tuggle called his survival a miracle given the condition of the vehicle.

Brock is a husband and father of four children, all under the age of 14.

The Shondra May Cold Case Task Force

The third Blue Shield Award was presented as a group honor to the task force of retired and active investigators from central Mississippi who worked together to close one of the state’s longest-running cold cases.

Shondra May, 17, disappeared in February 1986 after leaving her shift at McDonald’s. Her body was recovered 22 days later near Bolton in Hinds County. The case went unsolved for nearly four decades despite persistent investigative efforts.

Scott County Sheriff Mike Lee, who was 16 years old when May disappeared, came into office resolved to find an answer. Retired Rankin County Detective Greg Eklund had presented the case to a class at the Mississippi Law Enforcement Officers Training Academy and they had given the case fresh eyes.

This led to a group of retired investigators who began a renewed effort to solve the case. Working with active investigators from Scott County, the group built the case that led to the arrest of Rubin Weeks, who had been among the original suspects in the case and was convicted of a strikingly similar crime in Missouri in 1991.

Weeks was arrested in 2025, nearly 39 years after May’s disappearance.

The award was accepted by Lee, Eklund, and retired investigator Michael Frazier.

Officer Kenneth Cole Morgan — Pearl Police Department

Morgan, a K9 officer with the Pearl Police Department, was recognized for his work in steering a young woman battling opioid addiction toward recovery rather than simply processing her through the criminal justice system.

Pearl officers responded three times in a single week to a home where a woman in her early 20s had overdosed on fentanyl. On the third call, narcotics investigators charged her with possession of a controlled substance. Morgan, drawing on connections from his time in Alabama, secured her a spot in a residential recovery program.

On his day off, joined by his 5-year-old son and fellow investigators, he met the woman at the Rankin County Jail following her release and helped reunite her with her mother, who drove her to North Alabama for treatment.

The woman completed the program, and Morgan and several investigators traveled four hours to attend her graduation. She has since chosen to remain at the facility an additional year as a sponsor to others entering recovery. Program leaders say she is on track to earn certifications in addiction support.

Pearl Police Department Chief Nick McLendon submitted a commendation letter on Morgan’s behalf, noting his “professionalism, integrity, and commitment” and describing him as “a valuable asset” to the department and the community.

Officer Grant Holley — Horn Lake Police Department

Holley, a member of the Horn Lake Police Department’s Crisis Intervention Team, was recognized for two separate incidents in which he used de-escalation skills to safely disarm individuals in mental health crises.

In the first incident, officers were called to a home where a woman reported her brother had a handgun and was threatening to harm himself. Holley arrived to find the man in the kitchen with the weapon. After approximately 15 minutes of sustained conversation, Holley convinced the man to put the gun down. The man was later transported for professional mental health treatment.

Ten months earlier, Holley had responded to a nearly identical situation, again successfully de-escalating a subject in crisis and ensuring the individual received the help he needed.

Horn Lake PD noted in a public statement that the calls were “handled with grace and compassion” and credited Holley’s specialized training as central to both outcomes.

Holley was unable to attend the ceremony, and will receive his award in coming weeks.

item.title: Oktibbeha County deputies warn residents as scam reports continue - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Morgan Howard
item.description:
OKTIBBEHA COUNTY – The Oktibbeha County Sheriff’s Department is urging residents, especially older adults, to stay alert as scammers continue targeting people in the area and costing victims thousands of dollars.

In a public warning, the sheriff’s department said nearly every week people fall victim to scams, prompting repeated reports to investigators.

Officials said the department’s investigations division continues to look into the cases, but deputies are emphasizing prevention in hopes of stopping the crimes before more people lose money.

According to the sheriff’s department, scammers are becoming increasingly convincing and are making themselves appear more legitimate than in the past. Deputies said some scammers are now using existing business email addresses, websites and phone numbers to make their schemes seem real.

The department urged anyone who suspects they may be dealing with a scam to hang up and contact local law enforcement before responding further.

Officials said residents should tell law enforcement what the caller or sender is saying and ask whether the situation appears to be a scam.

item.title: NPS releases report on former Ridgeland firing range, seeks public comment - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Therese Apel
item.description:
TUPELO — The National Park Service on Friday released a report detailing environmental conditions and proposed cleanup options for the former Ridgeland Firing Range along the Natchez Trace Parkway, opening a 30-day public comment period.

The report, known as an Engineering Evaluation/Cost Analysis, outlines possible contamination at the site and presents a recommended plan for addressing it. An accompanying administrative record file includes documents and data used to develop the report.

The firing range operated from 1984 to 2002 in Ridgeland. The National Park Service is addressing the site under the Comprehensive Environmental Response, Compensation, and Liability Act, a federal law governing the cleanup of hazardous substances.

According to the agency, the report evaluates the nature and extent of contamination, potential risks to public health and the environment, and possible cleanup alternatives. The effort is being conducted as a non-time critical removal action, meaning officials have at least six months to plan before cleanup activities begin.

The public can review the report and administrative record online at parkplanning.nps.gov/RidgelandRange or in person at the Natchez Trace Parkway Visitor Center, 2680 Natchez Trace Parkway in Tupelo, during regular business hours Monday through Friday.

Comments will be accepted from April 3 through May 3 and can be submitted through the project website. Requests to extend the comment period by 15 days must be submitted before May 3 via email to [email protected] .

All comments will become part of the public record. While commenters may request that personal identifying information be withheld, the National Park Service said it cannot guarantee confidentiality.

item.title: National Pony Express Day celebrates daring riders, rapid news delivery of the Old West - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Therese Apel
item.description:
April 3 marks National Pony Express Day, a tribute to one of the most legendary and short-lived mail systems in American history.

The Pony Express was a service that played a crucial role in delivering news across a rapidly expanding nation. It’s understandable why we’d like to commemorate one of the first ways people got their long-distance news, and needless to say, it was a lot more dangerous back then. Breaking news was slower, but much harder-fought than it is now.

According to NationalToday.com, today we honor the founders and fearless riders of the mail delivery system on horseback that revolutionized communication in the early 1860s. Beyond letters, the service became a vital pipeline for newspapers and breaking news, helping keep the East and West informed at a time when the country was on the brink of the Civil War.

The Pony Express officially began operations on April 3, 1860, at a time when the country lacked a fast, reliable way to send messages across vast distances. NationalToday.com says the service emerged in response to California’s population surge during the Gold Rush, when prospectors, investors and businesses needed quicker communication with the East.

According to Britannica.com, the demand for faster delivery was driven in part by the need for timely news, as existing methods could take weeks. With tensions rising ahead of the Civil War, rapid transmission of information became increasingly important, making the Pony Express an essential link for newspapers and businesses trying to stay current.

The system was founded by freighting entrepreneurs Alexander Majors, William Russell and William B. Waddell, operating under the name Central Overland California and Pikes Peak Express Company. At its peak, the operation employed thousands and used extensive infrastructure, including horses, relay stations and supply networks, to move mail across the frontier, according to NationalToday.com.

What made the Pony Express remarkable was its speed. Messages that once took weeks or months to reach the West Coast could now be delivered in about 10 days. NationalToday.com notes one famous delivery, carrying President Abraham Lincoln’s inaugural address, arrived in just seven days and 17 hours.

According to Britannica.com, the Pony Express relied on a relay system of riders traveling a nearly 2,000-mile route from St. Joseph, Missouri, to Sacramento, California, with mail continuing to San Francisco by steamer. Riders typically covered 75 to 100 miles each, switching horses every 10 to 15 miles at roughly 190 stations scattered across rugged terrain.

The service was both efficient and dangerous. Britannica.com says riders faced harsh weather, difficult landscapes and threats of attack, yet the system lost only one bag of mail during its 18 months of operation. (That feels a little more reliable than now, doesn’t it?) Young, lightweight riders were preferred to maximize speed, and many became folk heroes of the American West.

Among them were figures like William “Buffalo Bill” Cody and Robert “Pony Bob” Haslam, whose endurance and daring helped cement the Pony Express in American folklore. Britannica.com notes that their exploits captured the national imagination and made the service one of the most colorful chapters in Western history.

Despite its success in speed and reliability, the Pony Express was financially unsustainable. NationalToday.com reports the company struggled with mounting costs and ultimately shut down on Oct. 24, 1861, just as the transcontinental telegraph made near-instant communication possible.

Britannica.com adds that the telegraph’s completion rendered the service obsolete, bringing an abrupt end to the Pony Express after just 18 months. Still, its impact was lasting.

The Pony Express helped pave the way for a unified, year-round transcontinental communication system, influencing how information and goods moved across the country.

Today, National Pony Express Day serves as a reminder of the ingenuity and grit that defined an era, and of the riders who raced against time to deliver not just mail, but the news that kept a growing nation connected.

item.title: Mississippi officials recognize Child Abuse Prevention Month, highlight training institute for frontline workers - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Morgan Howard
item.description:
JACKSON – Attorney General Lynn Fitch, Children’s Advocacy Centers of Mississippi and the Mississippi Department of Child Protection Services are recognizing April as Child Abuse Prevention Month and highlighting a training program designed to strengthen the state’s response to abuse cases.

Fitch, Children’s Advocacy Centers of Mississippi CEO Karla Steckler Tye and Department of Child Protection Services Commissioner Andrea Sanders toured the Child Advocacy Training Institute, a facility that provides hands-on, simulation-based training for students and professionals who may encounter child abuse cases.

State leaders said the institute is intended to help frontline workers better recognize, respond to and prevent child abuse by preparing them for real-world situations in a controlled environment.

“Receiving specialized training on recognizing, responding to, and preventing child abuse is critical for a strong response to child abuse,” Fitch said in a statement. She said the institute helps prepare the workforce that serves as the first line of defense for children experiencing abuse.

Tye said the protection and healing of abused children often depends on how professionals respond in critical moments, and she said the training institute gives them a chance to practice before facing those situations in real life.

Sanders said the facility allows Child Protection Services employees to walk through the full continuum of a case in a realistic, hands-on setting, strengthening how the system responds when abuse is reported.

In addition to touring the institute, Fitch and Children’s Advocacy Centers of Mississippi also shared child safety resources, including a new card offering tips for safe online gaming.

Officials said the card is the third in a series of resources created by the Attorney General’s Office and Children’s Advocacy Centers of Mississippi. The attorney general’s office also pointed to other online safety materials developed through its #BeAwareBeforeYouShare campaign, which focuses on raising awareness about the effects of social media on children’s mental and physical well-being.

item.title: MDOC K-9 officer killed while working perimeter at Marshall County Correctional Facility - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Morgan Howard
item.description:
MARSHALL COUNTY – The Marshall County Correctional Facility is mourning the loss of one of its K-9 officers after the dog was found fatally wounded while on duty, according to the Mississippi Department of Corrections.

Prison officials said K-9 Officer Floki was found dead Thursday morning. Investigators believe the 7-year-old Dutch shepherd was shot around 7:45 p.m. Wednesday while working the back perimeter of the prison to help prevent contraband from entering the facility.

The Mississippi Bureau of Investigation and the Holly Springs Police Department are investigating the case alongside the facility’s Corrections Investigation Division.

K-9 Commander Josh Russell found Floki when he went to bring the dog food and water, officials said.

According to the Department of Corrections, Floki was a multipurpose K-9 used for tracking, narcotics detection and other assignments.

Corrections Commissioner Burl Cain is offering a $1,000 reward for information leading to the arrest and conviction of the person or people responsible.

“It’s a shame to kill a defenseless dog who was doing his job to help us keep contraband out of the prison,” Cain said.

Cain noted that killing or injuring a public service animal is a felony in Mississippi, punishable by up to a $5,000 fine, five years in prison, or both.

Anyone with information is asked to contact Marshall County Correctional Facility Superintendent Frank Caswell or the prison’s Corrections Investigation Division at 662-252-7111.

item.title: Good Friday Devotional: "Not My will, but Yours." - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Therese Apel
item.description:
“𝐅𝐚𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫, 𝐢𝐟 𝐲𝐨𝐮 𝐚𝐫𝐞 𝐰𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐧𝐠, 𝐭𝐚𝐤𝐞 𝐭𝐡𝐢𝐬 𝐜𝐮𝐩 𝐟𝐫𝐨𝐦 𝐦𝐞; 𝐲𝐞𝐭 𝐧𝐨𝐭 𝐦𝐲 𝐰𝐢𝐥𝐥, 𝐛𝐮𝐭 𝐲𝐨𝐮𝐫𝐬 𝐛𝐞 𝐝𝐨𝐧𝐞.” — 𝐋𝐮𝐤𝐞 𝟐𝟐:𝟒𝟐

There is a garden in the middle of the worst night in human history. Did you ever think about that? That Jesus was born in a barn and betrayed in a garden? Normal places, but so symbolic. God sure knows how to paint His stories with nuance.

Jesus had just shared a final meal with the people He loved most. He had washed their feet and broken bread and passed the cup and tried to prepare them for something that would level them and they wouldn’t understand until later. And then He walked out into the dark, to a place called Gethsemane.

That garden was at the bottom of the Mount of Olives, and I need you to think about the history there: This is the same mountain where David fled when his son Absalom betrayed him, and the mountain where Zechariah prophesied Jesus would return. It is maybe the most theologically loaded hillside in human history.

Did you know that “Gethsemane” means “oil press?” It’s a mechanism they use to crush olives to produce something valuable. I don’t think that’s a coincidence.

He knelt down, and He prayed such a vulnerable, honest prayer, and He didn’t dress it up. He just fell on His knees in the dirt and in the original language, He called God “אַבָּא,” or “Abba.” That’s a word small children used, equivalent to “daddy” or “papa.”

Essentially, He said, “Dad, if there’s any other way, please. Take this cup from me.”

The Son of the God who spoke the world into existence, the Savior who calmed the sea with His voice, asked His Dad if there was any other way. He felt the weight of what was coming. The physical agony, of course, but also the spiritual and cosmic weight of carrying every sin ever committed by every person who would ever live. Can you imagine? For that time, all the guilt, all the pain, all the temptation and hate and selfishness and longing and all the things that plague our human nature, all of that was HIS. In His most human and desperate and vulnerable moment, the name He reached for was the most intimate one He knew. In His full humanity, He asked His Dad if maybe He wouldn’t have to do this. 𝑃𝑙𝑒𝑎𝑠𝑒, 𝐷𝑎𝑑. God said no. Not with words, necessarily, but the cup didn’t pass.

The Bible tells us that God sent an angel, though, not to rescue Him or to reroute the plan, but to strengthen Him for what was ahead. God didn’t remove the suffering. He showed up inside of it. And then Jesus said the bravest thing anyone’s ever said in possibly the worst moment anyone’s ever had: “Not My will, but Yours be done.”

I have prayed some desperate prayers in my life. I’ve been on my knees asking God to change outcomes of the inevitable, to heal people I loved, to reroute plans that felt unbearable. I know some of you reading this are in a place just like that right now. You’re in your own garden, in your own dark night, asking God to please, please find another way.

And sometimes He does. Sometimes the cup moves and the miracle happens and you get to stand there in front of Him with tears streaming down your face in pure gratitude. But sometimes the angel comes to strengthen and comfort instead.

Just like with Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, sometimes God’s answer isn’t deliverance from the fire, but His presence inside it. He doesn’t always pass the cup but sometimes instead gives us the strength to drink it.

And here’s what I’ve learned, more often reluctantly than not: That kind of answer requires more trust than the miracle does. It requires you to loosen your grip on the outcome and really believe that He is good even when the cup is bitter.

Not my will, but yours. Do what’s best here, Dad, no matter what my cost.

That sentence is the hinge all of history swings on, primarily in the garden that night, but also in every moment we face something we didn’t choose and can’t control. It’s the declaration of a faith that has moved past asking God to be our helper and into trusting Him as our Dad.

Jesus made it through Gethsemane. And because He drank that cup all the way to the bottom, Sunday was coming.

But you know what? Romans 8:15 and Galatians 4:6 both tell us that the Holy Spirit living inside us causes us to cry out, “Abba, Father,” as well. The same word, and the same intimacy. The Apostle Paul is saying in those passages that because of what happened after Gethsemane, because of Jesus’s suffering at the cross and the victory of the resurrection, we as believers are adopted into the same relationship Jesus had with His Dad.

Abba. We get to use that word too. We get to come to God in the dirt on our knees in our worst hour in the dark and call Him Dad and know He hears us.

Whatever garden you’re in right now, whatever cup you’re holding, whatever prayer you’ve prayed that hasn’t moved the mountain yet, He is with you in it. And Sunday is still coming.

Abba, not my will. Yours.

item.title: Byram police to increase enforcement with holiday safety operation - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Therese Apel
item.description:
BYRAM — The Byram Police Department will ramp up enforcement efforts across the city this week as part of a public safety initiative ahead of the Easter holiday weekend.

Operation Keep Byram Safe is scheduled to run April 2 through April 4 and will feature an increased and highly visible police presence, officials said. The initiative is aimed at deterring crime, improving traffic safety and ensuring residents and visitors can travel safely during a period of expected higher traffic.

Police said the operation will include coordinated efforts with additional law enforcement partners, along with a range of enforcement strategies. Officers will conduct safety checkpoints at various locations, verify and serve outstanding warrants and focus on apprehending individuals wanted by law enforcement.

High-visibility patrols will also be deployed throughout the city to provide a quicker response to incidents and reassure the public, according to the department.

With more people expected to travel during the holiday weekend, officials said the initiative is designed to promote safe driving practices and reduce the likelihood of accidents.

item.title: Annual festival showcases MC’s international students - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Therese Apel
item.description:
International students enrich Mississippi College’s culture in a variety of ways, including by sharing unique aspects of their home customs and traditions with their fellow students.

Through captivating presentations and artistic stage performances, the annual International Festival at MC showcases these students’ immense talents.

Sponsored by MC’s International Institute, the 2026 event is scheduled from 6:30 to 8:30 p.m. on Thursday, April 9, in Nelson Hall’s Swor Auditorium on the Clinton campus.

Richard Ladner, director of the International Institute, said the festival is the largest international event on campus and the institute’s only performance-oriented program.

“Our students come from a variety of cultures, and they are excited to share their traditions with the people of Mississippi,” Ladner said. “It’s a great opportunity for them to demonstrate artistic endeavors they are passionate about. The audience will have a rare opportunity to see performers from so many countries live and in person. It will be a fantastic night.”

The international students will celebrate aspects of their heritage in three-to-five-minute programs that educate audience members about the fashion, music and customs associated with their respective communities. Proceeds from the festival help support international student scholarships at MC.

Timothy Young, a Master of Accountancy student from Kingston, Jamaica, and an MC track and field athlete who will serve as emcee of this year’s event, said the International Festival highlights the international student population at Mississippi College.

“The International Festival is more than just an event: it is an opportunity for students to share a part of who they are with the campus community,” said Young, who serves as president of the International Student Association at MC. “Events like this help build connections, break down cultural barriers and create a stronger sense of unity among students of all backgrounds.

“My favorite aspect of the festival is the cultural exchange – being able to experience different cultures through traditions and perspectives. It’s an important part of MC’s culture because it highlights and celebrates the diversity of our student body. It reflects MC as a global university.”

As in past festivals, this year’s event will include a crowd-favorite fashion show featuring authentic clothing from a variety of countries, student performances, and guest performers, including dancers from Ballet Magnificat in Jackson and the Southern Pine Singers representing the Mississippi Band of Choctaw Indians in Philadelphia.

“The International Festival is a great way for MC’s international students to continue to forge friendships and relationships with the community,” Ladner added. “It’s also a great way for community members to be exposed to the broader world around them and to witness the broad tapestry of people from different backgrounds at MC.”

Following the festival, audience members will have an opportunity to interact with the performers during a reception in the Nelson Hall lobby. Refreshments will be available.

Tickets to the International Festival cost $10 each for adults, $5 each for students and $25 for families of any size. They may be purchased in advance or at the door. For more information or to purchase tickets, visit mc.edu/international/events/international-festival .

item.title: Animal Control Rescues dog with severe neck wounds wandering in Lee County - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Morgan Howard
item.description:
LEE COUNTY – A dog with severe neck injuries is recovering after being found wandering along a roadside in Plantersville, according to North Mississippi Animal Care and Control Association LLC.

The organization said one of its officers was patrolling in Lee County when the dog was spotted walking along the side of the road in the Town of Plantersville.

Officials said the dog was not in a yard and was roaming freely. The animal had no collar, identification tags or microchip, making it impossible to immediately identify an owner.

Because Plantersville has a leash ordinance, the officer stopped and called the dog over, authorities said.

When the officer examined the dog, the injuries appeared severe. According to the organization, the dog had significant wounds around her neck, and it appeared she had been tied with a cable or rope that became embedded, causing deep lacerations and extreme pain.

Despite her condition, the dog was described as gentle and came willingly to the officer.

She was transported to the shelter, where she is now receiving medical treatment, medication and supportive care, officials said.

North Mississippi Animal Care and Control Association said the case is a reminder of the dangers of improperly restraining dogs and warned that tying an animal out incorrectly can lead to serious injury or death.

item.title: Veteran Jackson County deputy killed in line of duty Wednesday - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Therese Apel
item.description:
JACKSON COUNTY — A Jackson County Sheriff’s deputy died early Wednesday morning after being shot while responding to a disturbance call.

The incident occurred at an apartment complex in St. Martin.

Deputy Michael Jimerson was transported to Ocean Springs Hospital following the shooting, where he later died of his injuries. He was 36 years into a life built on service to others.

According to the Jackson County Sheriff’s Office, deputies were dispatched at approximately 11:00 p.m. on April 1, to a reported disturbance at the Reserve Apartments in St. Martin. An exchange of gunfire occurred involving a female individual, who was pronounced deceased at the scene.

The Mississippi Bureau of Investigation is handling the ongoing investigation, and no further details about the circumstances of the shooting have been released at this time.

Deputy Jimerson first joined the Jackson County Sheriff’s Office as a reserve deputy in 2010, before being hired full-time in 2014. He served in the Patrol Division, answering calls at all hours, in all conditions, for people in their worst moments.

His colleagues remembered him Wednesday night not just as a fellow officer but as a trusted friend. The Sheriff’s Office described him as earning the respect of those around him through professionalism, dedication, and compassion.

The Jackson County Sheriff’s Office has asked for prayers for Deputy Jimerson’s family, friends, and the men and women of the department as they grieve. The Mississippi Bureau of Investigation has offered no timeline on the completion of its investigation.

Deputy Michael Jimerson served Jackson County for more than a decade. He answered the call on Wednesday night. He should be remembered as a hero for both.

item.title: Quinton Tellis trial to resume in Louisiana May 13 - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Therese Apel
item.description:
MONROE, La. — The murder trial of Quinton Tellis is set to resume May 13 in Ouachita Parish following a pause after the first week of testimony in the 2015 killing of Ming Chen Hsiao.

The bench trial, which began in March, was expected to last only a few days but was halted due to scheduling conflicts, with prosecutors indicating additional witnesses still need to testify. The defense has indicated that they have one witness as well.

SEE QUINTON TELLIS COVERAGE FROM DARKHORSE PRESS

Tellis is accused of fatally stabbing Hsiao, a University of Louisiana Monroe graduate student known to her friends as Mandy, inside her apartment in July 2015. He has also been identified as a primary suspect in the 2014 death of Jessica Chambers in Mississippi.

During the first week of testimony, prosecutors presented evidence and witness accounts aimed at tying Tellis to the killing, including testimony from a key witness who said Tellis admitted to stabbing a woman to obtain her debit card PIN.

Judge Larry Jefferson also heard from a forensic pathologist who detailed the severity of Hsiao’s injuries , testifying that she suffered 30 stab wounds, including three fatal wounds to the neck.

Other testimony focused on inconsistencies in Tellis’ statements to investigators. A man identified in court as someone Tellis claimed was involved in the case testified that he had minimal contact with Tellis and denied key elements of Tellis’ account, casting doubt on the defense narrative.

Additional witnesses placed Tellis at or near Hsiao’s apartment in the days leading up to her death, with one neighbor testifying that an encounter with him “creeped her out” at the time.

Despite extensive testimony, prosecutors have not yet called all of their witnesses, including individuals expected to address key elements of the timeline and forensic evidence. The defense is also expected to present at least one expert witness to challenge cell phone and digital aspects of the state’s case.

Tellis remains in custody as the trial awaits its next phase in May.

item.title: One MSU alum manages Artemis II mission as a second supports its readiness - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Special to Darkhorse Press
item.description:
STARKVILLE — It’s a long way from Hernando, Mississippi, to Kennedy Space Center, but Matthew Ramsey’s decision to spend a few years in-between the two at Mississippi State University made the trip worth it.

Today, Ramsey is celebrating the success of Wednesday’s launch of NASA’s Artemis II mission—the first crewed mission since 1972—as its mission manager. The 10-day expedition from Earth around the moon marks a major step toward returning humans to the lunar surface and setting the stage for long-term exploration.

The North Mississippi native enrolled at Mississippi State in the early 1990s as a pitcher for the university baseball team while earning a 1992 bachelor’s and 1993 master’s degree in aerospace engineering. He began his work with NASA in 2002.

He said in one of the agency’s website stories, “There are a lot of similarities between mission management and pitching. You control many aspects of the tempo, and there’s a lot of weight on your shoulders.”

On this history-making mission, that responsibility includes pre-launch daily preparations, addressing issues as deputy of the Artemis II management team, and resolving any flight changes.

One of his NASA interview comments about his immeasurable duties was, “Most of my time is focused on making sure we’re ready to fly astronauts Reid, Victor, Christina and Jeremy to the Moon and bring them home safely.”

Also involved with the success of Artemis II is Parker Glass, who works for NASA’s Exploration Ground Systems and has been overseeing budget development, project plans and resource allocation in preparation for Wednesday’s launch.

Glass was exposed to NASA and space exploration during most of his childhood in Yorktown, Virginia, where his dad was employed at Langley Research Center for many years. Glass became enamored with becoming an astronaut, but as he got older his interests changed.

He discovered the prestigious PGA Golf Management program at Mississippi State, one of just 16 in the nation. He said in a NASA article, “I first visited MSU in 2014 and fell in love with Starkville.”

After eventually changing his major to finance, he was surprised to discover there were internship opportunities with NASA and that brought him back to his original passion.

Glass wants students interested in NASA and the agency’s work to know that being an astronaut doesn’t have to factor into the equation of working in space exploration. “NASA needs everybody,” he said.

He graduated from MSU in 2018 with a bachelor’s in business administration and earned a Master of Business Administration degree in 2022.

item.title: Mississippi schools to face higher accountability standards beginning in 2025-26 - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Morgan Howard
item.description:
Mississippi schools and districts will face higher standards for earning accountability grades beginning with the 2025-26 school year, and those grades will establish a new baseline for measuring performance across the state, according to the Mississippi Department of Education.

The department said accountability grades to be released in fall 2026 will not be directly comparable to grades from previous years because of the tougher benchmarks.

As a result, many schools and districts could receive lower letter grades than they earned in 2024-25, even if student performance remains the same or improves on state assessments, the department said.

Mississippi law requires accountability standards to increase when 75% of students are proficient or when 65% of schools or districts earn a grade of B or higher. State officials said that milestone was reached in 2023, when 74% of schools and 71% of districts earned an A or B, compared with 37% for both in 2016.

“Mississippi students and schools have made extraordinary progress, and that progress is exactly why state law requires us to raise the bar,” State Superintendent of Education Lance Evans said in a statement.

The Mississippi Department of Education said it worked for two years with its Accountability Task Force, Technical Advisory Committee and a special Standard Setting Task Force to revise the accountability system. The Mississippi State Board of Education approved the updated standards in November 2025.

Accountability grades are based on multiple measures of student achievement, including statewide assessment results in English language arts, math and science, progress of English learners, performance in advanced courses and career and technical education programs, and graduation rates.

The department said the most significant change for 2025-26 is the higher number of points schools and districts will need to earn each letter grade.

Another change beginning in 2025-26 is the addition of a new Mississippi Readiness Index, which replaces previous college and career readiness measures for high schools and districts. The index includes student performance on the ACT, SAT, ACT WorkKeys and the Armed Services Vocational Aptitude Battery, as well as success in Advanced Placement, dual credit, dual enrollment and career and technical education programs, industry certifications, diploma endorsements, and on-time and five-year graduation rates.

The department also said the U.S. history assessment will no longer count in accountability measures, and annual goals for English learner progress have been updated.

State assessment results for the 2025-26 school year are expected to be released in August 2026. Accountability grades will follow in fall 2026 and will include a breakdown of the components that make up each school or district’s score.

Evans said families and communities should look beyond the overall letter grade when evaluating school performance under the new system.
